title: The claim
text: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
body: Christianity does not begin with a moral code. It begins with a person making a claim about himself that is either true or arrogant, and cannot be anything in between.

Jesus does not say he teaches the way. He says he is it. Every other founder of a religion pointed away from themselves towards something; this one points at himself and says the Father is reached through him.
That is worth facing squarely before anything else in this path. If the claim is false, nothing that follows matters. If it is true, nothing else matters as much.
question: Have you ever decided what you think of that claim — or only inherited an answer?
practice: Read John 14 in full this week. It is one conversation, and it is short.
prayer: Jesus, if this is true, I want to know it. Show me who you are.

title: The problem
text: for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God;
body: Paul has spent two chapters proving that the religious and the irreligious are in the same position, and this is the sentence that lands it. Not most. All.

Sin in the Bible is less a list of infractions than a direction — a life curved in on itself. That is why the good and the obviously bad end up in the same sentence: the difference between them is real, and it is not large enough to matter at this distance.
This is the least flattering thing Christianity says, and it is also the reason its offer is free. A diagnosis nobody escapes makes a cure nobody earns.
question: Where do you quietly rank yourself against other people to feel all right?
practice: Name one thing you have justified for years. Do not fix it yet — just stop calling it something else.
prayer: God, I have graded myself on a curve. I would rather see it as you see it.

title: What the cross did
text: Because Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God; being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit;
body: Peter puts the whole transaction in one line: the righteous for the unrighteous, once, to bring you to God. Not to make God willing — to bring you in.
Once matters. A sacrifice that has to be repeated is a sacrifice that did not finish the job, and the whole letter to the Hebrews is an argument that this one did.
And the purpose is a relationship, not an acquittal. The point of the cross is not that a file was closed; it is that a person was brought home.
question: Do you relate to God as someone acquitted, or as someone brought in?
practice: Read the account of the crucifixion in Luke 23 slowly, as news rather than liturgy.
prayer: Jesus, you did this once and it was enough. Bring me to the Father.

title: Grace, not performance
text: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.
body: Two words carry this: gift, and boast. If any part of it were earned, there would be something to boast about, and Paul closes that door on purpose.

Most people who have been in church a long time can recite this and still live as though God's welcome tracked their week. The test is what happens after you fail — whether you assume you are further away.
You are not. That is the whole point of calling it grace.
question: What do you unconsciously do to make God like you more?
practice: Next time you fail this week, come to God the same day rather than after a decent interval.
prayer: Father, I keep trying to pay for something already given. Teach me to receive it.

title: What you now are
text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
body: Paul is not describing how a Christian feels on a good day. He is describing a change of category — the same word used for God making the world.
The change is announced before it is complete, which is why an honest Christian life contains both real transformation and real failure. You are new; you are not yet finished.
That gap is not hypocrisy. It is the ordinary shape of the thing, and knowing it stops you giving up the first time the old self is obviously still there.
question: Which old thing do you still treat as your identity?
practice: Write down one habit you assumed you would never be free of. Pray about it by name.
prayer: God, I am new in Christ and still learning to live like it. Finish what you started.

title: How this life is lived
text: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
body: The first church's entire programme is four things, and none of them can be done alone. Teaching, one another, the table, prayer.
Continued steadfastly is the load-bearing phrase. This is not four experiences they had; it is four things they kept doing when the novelty wore off, which is what turns belief into a life.
A faith practised only on a phone is missing at least two of the four. This app is a help; it is not a church, and it will keep saying so.
question: Which of the four is currently missing from your week?
practice: Put the missing one in your calendar this week, with a person's name attached.
prayer: Lord, keep me steady in the ordinary four. Give me people to do them with.
